subtopics.title: Transport Service, TCP & UDP
subtopics.subtitle: Process-to-process delivery, TCP and UDP headers, their differences and SCTP

concepts.text: The Transport Service

The transport layer (layer 4 of OSI, and of the five-layer TCP/IP model) provides process-to-process delivery: it carries a message from a process (running program) on one host to the correct process on another host. The network layer (IP) only delivers packets host to host, so the transport layer adds port numbers to tell processes apart. It is the first truly end-to-end layer: transport entities exist only in the two end hosts, never in routers. The unit of data is called a segment in TCP and a user datagram in UDP.
Services a transport layer can offer to applications:
items: Connection-oriented service: a connection is set up, data is transferred and the connection is released (TCP, SCTP).
Connectionless service: each message is sent independently with no setup (UDP).
Reliable delivery: lost or corrupted data is detected and retransmitted using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and timers.
In-order delivery: data is handed to the application in the order it was sent, even if segments arrive out of order.
Flow control (do not overrun the receiver) and congestion control (do not overrun the network).
Multiplexing and demultiplexing of many application processes over one IP address using port numbers.

concepts.text: TCP: Transmission Control Protocol

TCP (RFC 793) is a connection-oriented, reliable, byte-stream protocol. It treats application data as a continuous stream of bytes, numbers every byte with a 32-bit sequence number, and uses cumulative acknowledgements, retransmission timers, a sliding window for flow control, and congestion control. Connections are full duplex and point to point, set up with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and released with a four-way FIN/ACK exchange. HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), FTP (20/21), SSH (22), Telnet (23) and SMTP (25) run over TCP.

rows: Identify the sending and receiving processes
Number of the first data byte in this segment (ISN during SYN)
Next byte expected from the other side (valid when ACK = 1)
HLEN counts 4-byte words (5 to 15); six control flags
Receive window (rwnd) in bytes, used for flow control
Error check over pseudo-header + segment; end of urgent data

concepts.text: The six classic TCP control flags:
items: URG: the urgent pointer field is valid.
ACK: the acknowledgement number field is valid (set on every segment after the first SYN).
PSH: push the data to the application immediately instead of buffering it.
RST: reset (abort) the connection immediately.
SYN: synchronise sequence numbers to open a connection.
FIN: the sender has finished sending data (starts connection release).

concepts.plainText: TCP header length = HLEN x 4 bytes, between 20 and 60 bytes

concepts.text: UDP: User Datagram Protocol

UDP (RFC 768) is a connectionless, unreliable, message-oriented protocol that adds almost nothing to IP except port numbers and an optional checksum. Its header is a fixed 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length (header + data) and checksum, each 16 bits. There is no handshake, no acknowledgement, no retransmission, no ordering, no flow control and no congestion control, so it has low overhead and low delay. It suits short request-reply exchanges (DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, SNMP 161/162, TFTP 69), real-time media (VoIP, video streaming, online games) and multicast or broadcast traffic.

rows: Web pages must arrive complete; DNS query is one short exchange
Files and sessions need reliability; bootstrapping needs simplicity
Mail must not be lost; management polls are small and periodic
A late retransmitted voice packet is useless, so loss is tolerated

concepts.text: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol, RFC 4960) is a third transport protocol that combines features of both. It is message-oriented like UDP but reliable and connection-oriented like TCP. It supports multi-streaming (several independent streams in one association, avoiding head-of-line blocking) and multi-homing (an endpoint can have several IP addresses for failover). It uses a four-way handshake with a cookie to resist SYN-flood style attacks and is used for telephony signalling (SIGTRAN).

Both TCP and UDP compute their checksum over a 12-byte pseudo-header plus the segment. The pseudo-header contains the source IP address, destination IP address, a zero byte, the protocol number (6 for TCP, 17 for UDP) and the TCP/UDP length. It is not transmitted; it is only used in the calculation so that a segment delivered to the wrong host or protocol is detected. The checksum is mandatory in TCP, optional in UDP over IPv4 (all zeros means not computed) and mandatory for UDP over IPv6.
Going Deeper: TCP and UDP in Detail

A handy way to picture the two protocols: TCP is like registered mail, where every item is tracked and the sender learns that it arrived, while UDP is like dropping an ordinary letter in a post box and hoping it gets there. TCP is connection-oriented, reliable and ordered, and it controls both its sending rate and the load it puts on the network, so it is slower to start and carries more overhead. UDP skips all of this, which makes it fast and light but leaves loss, duplication and reordering for the application to handle. Choose TCP when every byte must arrive correctly (web pages, e-mail, file transfer, remote login) and UDP when a late packet is worse than a lost one or when the exchange is one short query (voice and video calls, online games, live broadcasts, DNS lookups).
Corrections and updates to common study-note claims:
items: TCP 'error correction' does not mean that TCP repairs bits. A segment that fails the checksum is discarded silently; the sender notices the missing acknowledgement and retransmits, so recovery is by retransmission (ARQ), not by an error-correcting code.
UDP does detect errors: its 16-bit checksum over the pseudo-header, header and data lets the receiver throw away a damaged datagram. What UDP never does is retransmit it.

On-demand streaming such as Netflix and YouTube is mostly delivered over HTTP, that is over TCP or over QUIC, because the player buffers several seconds ahead and hides retransmissions. UDP with RTP is the usual choice for interactive, real-time media: VoIP, video calls and fast online games.

TCP is now specified by RFC 9293 (2022), which replaced RFC 793, and SCTP (IP protocol number 132) by RFC 9260, which replaced RFC 4960; the header layouts and behaviour taught in textbooks are unchanged.
QUIC (RFC 9000), the transport under HTTP/3, runs on top of UDP but adds its own reliability, congestion control and TLS 1.3 encryption, so 'runs over UDP' does not always mean 'unreliable'.

concepts.text: How TCP builds a reliable, ordered byte stream on top of best-effort IP:
items: Sequence numbers: every byte has a 32-bit number, so the receiver can put segments back in order and discard duplicates. The initial sequence number (ISN) is chosen randomly for each connection (RFC 6528).
Cumulative acknowledgements: the acknowledgement number names the next byte expected, which confirms everything before it in one value.
Checksum: it covers the pseudo-header, header and data, so damaged or misdelivered segments are dropped.
Retransmission: a retransmission timer (RTO) resends data that stays unacknowledged, and fast retransmit resends a segment as soon as three duplicate ACKs show it is missing.
Receive buffer and window: out-of-order data is held until the gap is filled, and the advertised window stops the sender from overrunning that buffer.
Connection state: the handshake agrees on both ISNs before data flows, and the FIN exchange makes sure all data has been delivered before the connection is closed.

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 2,500 bytes, MSS = 1,000, client ISN = 5,000
The SYN uses sequence number 5,000, so the first data byte is 5,001
Segment 1: seq 5,001   1,000 bytes = bytes 5,001..6,000  -> ACK 6,001
Segment 2: seq 6,001   1,000 bytes = bytes 6,001..7,000  -> ACK 7,001
Segment 3: seq 7,001     500 bytes = bytes 7,001..7,500  -> ACK 7,501
If segment 2 is lost and the receiver buffers out-of-order data:
  segment 3 arrives        -> duplicate ACK 6,001 (still waiting for byte 6,001)
  retransmitted segment 2  -> ACK 7,501 (the gap is filled)
The client's FIN would then carry sequence number 7,501

Worked example 2: UDP checksum, 192.168.0.1:8080 -> 192.168.0.2:53, data "OK"
Pseudo-header : C0A8 0001 C0A8 0002 0011 000A  (zero + protocol 17, UDP length 10)
UDP header    : 1F90 0035 000A 0000            (ports 8080 and 53, length 10, checksum 0)
Data          : 4F4B                           ("O" = 4F, "K" = 4B)
Add all 11 words      : 1F088 (17 bits)
Fold the carry        : F088 + 1 = F089
Checksum              : ones' complement of F089 = 0F76
Receiver adds all 11 words with 0F76 in place: F089 + 0F76 = FFFF -> accepted

rows: Mark the end of the options / pad so the next option starts on a 4-byte boundary
Largest data block the sender of the option can receive in one segment; SYN only
Shift count S (0 to 14) applied to the 16-bit window field; SYN only
Reports up to 4 blocks of data received beyond a gap (3 when timestamps are also used)
RTT measurement and PAWS protection against wrapped sequence numbers

concepts.text: The 16-bit window field lets a sender have at most 65,535 bytes unacknowledged, so its throughput can never exceed 65,535 bytes per RTT. On a 100 Mbps path with an 80 ms RTT that is only about 6.6 Mbps, because keeping the pipe full needs a window equal to the bandwidth-delay product, 10^8 × 0.08 / 8 = 1,000,000 bytes. The window scale option (RFC 7323) solves this: both SYNs carry a shift count S, and every later window value is multiplied by 2^S, so S = 4 gives 65,535 × 16 = 1,048,560 bytes here, and the maximum S = 14 allows about 1 GiB. The MSS option solves a different problem: it keeps each segment small enough to fit in one IP packet on the path, so that no fragmentation is needed.

concepts.plainText: Effective window = window field W x 2^S, which must be at least bandwidth B x RTT (converted to bytes) to keep the pipe full; S = 0 to 14

rows: Reliable messages in one or more streams
Four-way handshake with a state cookie
Every data chunk (TSN) plus a per-stream number

concepts.text: Common mistakes and special cases:
items: The ACK number is the next byte expected, not the last byte received: after bytes 1 to 1,000 the ACK is 1,001.
SYN and FIN each use up one sequence number although they carry no data; a pure ACK uses none, so ACKs are never themselves acknowledged.
HLEN (data offset) counts 4-byte words, but the UDP length field counts bytes and includes the 8-byte header.
The MSS excludes both headers: MSS = MTU − 40 for IPv4 without options, which is 1,460 bytes on Ethernet. A host that receives no MSS option must assume 536 bytes (IPv4) or 1,220 bytes (IPv6).
TCP does not keep message boundaries: three 100-byte writes may be read as one 300-byte block, so applications must frame their own messages, while UDP delivers each datagram whole or not at all.
The pseudo-header is used only to compute the checksum and is never sent; because it contains the IP addresses, a NAT router that rewrites an address must also fix the TCP or UDP checksum.
Since RFC 3168 the TCP header has 4 reserved bits and 8 flags: CWR and ECE (for Explicit Congestion Notification) were added to URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN.

concepts.text: For any sequence-number question, write each segment as first byte..last byte: the next segment starts at last + 1, and that same value is the ACK for it. Add one extra number for a SYN or a FIN and none for a pure ACK, and remember that header-length fields are in 4-byte words while length fields are in bytes.

formulas.plainText: TCP header length = HLEN x 4 bytes (HLEN 5 to 15 gives 20 to 60 bytes)
UDP length = 8 + data; maximum UDP payload over IPv4 = 65535 - 8 - 20 = 65507 bytes
TCP sequence numbers are 32 bits, so 2^32 byte numbers before wrap-around

notes.text: Remember the sizes: TCP header 20 bytes minimum and 60 bytes maximum (HLEN field is in 4-byte words), UDP header always 8 bytes. Protocol numbers in the IP header: TCP = 6, UDP = 17, ICMP = 1.
DNS normally uses UDP port 53 for queries but switches to TCP port 53 for zone transfers and for responses too large for a single UDP message.
TCP numbers bytes, not segments. A segment with sequence number 1000 carrying 500 bytes holds bytes 1000 to 1499, and the receiver acknowledges it with ACK = 1500.

formulas.title: TCP header length
formulas.plainText: TCP header = HLEN x 4 bytes
formulas.description: The 4-bit HLEN field counts 32-bit words, so values 5 to 15 give a header of 20 to 60 bytes.

formulas.title: UDP length
formulas.plainText: UDP length = 8 + data bytes
formulas.description: The UDP length field covers the fixed 8-byte header plus the payload.

formulas.title: Acknowledgement number
formulas.plainText: ACK = sequence number + number of data bytes received
formulas.description: TCP acknowledges cumulatively by naming the next byte it expects to receive.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between host-to-host and process-to-process delivery?
flashcards.back: The network layer (IP) delivers packets between hosts using IP addresses; the transport layer delivers data to the correct process on that host using port numbers.

flashcards.front: What are the four fields of the UDP header?
flashcards.back: Source port, destination port, length and checksum, each 16 bits, giving a fixed 8-byte header.
A 12-byte structure (source IP, destination IP, zero, protocol, length) included only in the checksum calculation to detect misdelivered segments; it is never transmitted.

flashcards.front: Name two features of SCTP that TCP lacks.
flashcards.back: Multi-streaming (several independent streams in one association) and multi-homing (multiple IP addresses per endpoint); it is also message-oriented.

questions.questionText: The header length (HLEN) field of a TCP segment contains the value 8. What is the size of the TCP header?
questions.explanation: HLEN counts 4-byte words, so 8 x 4 = 32 bytes: the 20-byte fixed header plus 12 bytes of options.

questions.questionText: What is the size of the UDP header?
questions.explanation: The UDP header is a fixed 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length and checksum, 16 bits each.

questions.questionText: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is best described as:
questions.explanation: UDP sends each datagram on its own without setting up a connection, and it has no acknowledgements or retransmission, so delivery is not guaranteed. 'Unreliable' means no delivery guarantee; UDP still has a checksum to detect damaged datagrams.

questions.questionText: Which field in the TCP header lets the receiver put arriving data back into the correct order?
questions.explanation: Each segment's sequence number is the number of its first data byte, so the receiver can place segments that arrive out of order and discard duplicates. The acknowledgement number reports the next byte expected, and the window is used for flow control.

questions.questionText: Why is UDP called a connectionless protocol?
options: It encrypts every datagram at the transport layer
It communicates only with broadcast packets
It uses a different IP address for each datagram
It sends data without first setting up a connection, and handles every datagram independently
questions.explanation: UDP has no handshake and keeps no connection state: an application can send a datagram at once, and each datagram is handled on its own. It does not encrypt data, and it works with unicast as well as broadcast and multicast.

questions.questionText: Real-time applications such as VoIP normally carry their voice packets over UDP rather than TCP. What is the main reason?
options: A retransmitted voice packet would arrive too late to be played, so TCP's retransmission and in-order waiting only add delay
UDP retransmits lost voice packets faster than TCP does
TCP cannot send in both directions at once, which a phone call needs
UDP's header is larger, so it can carry the timing information that voice needs
questions.explanation: In a live conversation a packet that arrives late is useless, and TCP would also hold back later packets until the lost one is resent (head-of-line blocking). UDP, usually with RTP on top, never retransmits and accepts a little loss in exchange for low, steady delay; TCP is full duplex, and UDP's 8-byte header is smaller than TCP's.

questions.questionText: Which pair of protocols are both connection-oriented transport protocols?
questions.explanation: TCP sets up a connection with a three-way handshake, and SCTP sets up an association with a four-way handshake, before any data flows. UDP is connectionless, and ICMP is a network-layer helper protocol, not a transport protocol.

questions.questionText: Which set of mechanisms does TCP use to give reliable delivery over IP's best-effort service?
options: Forward error-correcting codes added to every segment
Sequence numbers, acknowledgements, checksums and retransmission of lost or damaged segments
Sending every segment twice over different routes
questions.explanation: TCP numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrives, detects damage with a checksum and retransmits anything not acknowledged in time, which is error recovery by retransmission (ARQ). It does not add error-correcting codes, and encryption is the job of TLS, not TCP.

questions.questionText: The network layer delivers an IP datagram to the correct host. What additional delivery does the transport layer provide?
options: Node-to-node delivery across a single link using MAC addresses
Conversion of domain names into IP addresses
Process-to-process delivery, using port numbers to reach the right application
questions.explanation: IP gets the datagram to the host; the transport layer then uses the destination port to hand the data to the correct process, such as a web server on port 80. Link-by-link delivery with MAC addresses is the data link layer's job, and name resolution is done by DNS.

questions.questionText: Which statement about where transport-layer protocols such as TCP and UDP run is correct?
options: They run only in the end hosts; routers normally process packets only up to the network layer
They run in every router along the path
They run only in layer-2 switches
They run only in the destination host, not in the source host
questions.explanation: Transport protocols are end-to-end: the TCP or UDP entities live in the two end systems, while routers forward packets using the IP header. Middleboxes such as NAT routers and firewalls may read port numbers, but they do not run the transport protocol on the hosts' behalf.

questions.questionText: A client calls send() three times on a TCP socket, with 100 bytes each time. Which statement about what the receiving application sees is correct?
options: It always reads exactly three separate 100-byte messages
It may read the three messages in a different order
It reads the 300 bytes in order, but in any grouping (for example one 300-byte read), because TCP does not preserve message boundaries
It can read the bytes only after the connection has been closed
questions.explanation: TCP delivers a reliable, ordered byte stream, so the bytes come out in the order they were sent, but how they are grouped into reads depends on segmenting and buffering. Applications over TCP must mark their own message boundaries; UDP, by contrast, delivers each datagram as a whole.

questions.questionText: Which of the following fields is NOT part of the UDP header?
questions.explanation: The 8-byte UDP header has only four 16-bit fields: source port, destination port, length and checksum. UDP has no sequence numbers because it neither orders nor retransmits data.

questions.questionText: A UDP datagram carries 1,000 bytes of application data. What value does its UDP length field contain?
questions.explanation: The UDP length covers the 8-byte header plus the data: 8 + 1,000 = 1,008 bytes. 1,028 would also add the 20-byte IPv4 header, which belongs in the IP total length, not in the UDP length.

questions.questionText: What is the largest amount of application data that a single UDP datagram can carry over IPv4, assuming a 20-byte IP header with no options?
questions.explanation: The 16-bit IPv4 total length allows at most 65,535 bytes, from which the 20-byte IP header and the 8-byte UDP header are taken: 65,535 − 20 − 8 = 65,507 bytes. 65,527 forgets the IP header and 65,515 forgets the UDP header.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the UDP checksum is correct?
options: It is mandatory over IPv4 but not used over IPv6
It can detect and correct single-bit errors
It covers only the 8-byte UDP header
It is optional over IPv4, where a value of 0 means that no checksum was computed, but it is required by default over IPv6
questions.explanation: Over IPv4 a sender may leave the checksum field as 0 (a computed result of 0 is sent as FFFF instead); IPv6 has no header checksum, so RFC 8200 makes the UDP checksum required by default. It covers the pseudo-header, the header and the data, and it only detects errors.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT part of the IPv4 pseudo-header used in the TCP and UDP checksum?
questions.explanation: The pseudo-header holds the source and destination IP addresses, a zero byte, the protocol number (6 for TCP, 17 for UDP) and the TCP/UDP length. TTL is left out because routers change it at every hop, which would make the end-to-end checksum fail.

questions.questionText: Which TCP flag asks the receiving TCP to pass the data to the application immediately instead of waiting for its buffer to fill?
questions.explanation: PSH (push) tells the receiver to deliver the data without further buffering. URG marks urgent data, RST aborts the connection and FIN starts closing it.

questions.questionText: Compute the UDP checksum of a datagram sent from 10.0.0.1, port 1234 (04D2 hex), to 10.0.0.5, port 69 (0045 hex), carrying the 2 data bytes "Hi" (4869 hex). Include the IPv4 pseudo-header (protocol 17 = 0011 hex) and treat the checksum field as 0000 during the calculation.
questions.explanation: The UDP length is 8 + 2 = 10 (000A). Adding 0A00 + 0001 + 0A00 + 0005 + 0011 + 000A (pseudo-header) + 04D2 + 0045 + 000A + 0000 (header) + 4869 (data) gives 61AB with no carry, and its ones' complement is 9E54. 61AB is the uncomplemented sum, B275 leaves out the pseudo-header and E6BD leaves out the data.

questions.questionText: An IPv4 datagram has a total length of 1,500 bytes and an IHL field of 6. It carries a TCP segment whose header length (data offset) field is 8. How many bytes of application data does the segment carry?
questions.explanation: IP header = IHL × 4 = 6 × 4 = 24 bytes and TCP header = 8 × 4 = 32 bytes, so the data is 1,500 − 24 − 32 = 1,444 bytes. 1,460 assumes 20-byte headers with no options, and 1,448 ignores the 4 bytes of IP options.

questions.questionText: A TCP receiver has just received a segment holding bytes 5,001 to 6,000, and all earlier bytes have already arrived. Which acknowledgement number does it send?
questions.explanation: TCP acknowledges cumulatively with the number of the next byte it expects: after byte 6,000 that is 6,001. ACK 6,000 would say that byte 6,000 itself has not arrived yet.

questions.questionText: A TCP sender transmits three segments: sequence number 1,000 (400 bytes), 1,400 (600 bytes) and 2,000 (500 bytes). The second segment is lost, and the receiver buffers out-of-order data. Which ACK does the receiver send when the third segment arrives, and which ACK does it send when the retransmitted second segment arrives?
questions.explanation: Segment 1 covers bytes 1,000 to 1,399, so the receiver expects 1,400; segment 3 (bytes 2,000 to 2,499) is buffered and the receiver repeats ACK 1,400 as a duplicate ACK. When the retransmitted bytes 1,400 to 1,999 fill the gap, everything up to byte 2,499 is present and the ACK jumps to 2,500.

questions.questionText: A client's SYN carries the initial sequence number 7,000. After the handshake the client sends three data segments of 500 bytes each. What is the sequence number of the third data segment?
questions.explanation: The SYN uses sequence number 7,000, so the first data byte is 7,001, and the third segment starts at 7,001 + 2 × 500 = 8,001. 8,000 forgets that the SYN consumes one number, and 7,003 wrongly numbers segments instead of bytes.

questions.questionText: A TCP sender transmits continuously at 10 Gbps (10^10 bit/s). About how long does its 32-bit sequence number space take to wrap around, and what follows, given a maximum segment lifetime (MSL) of 2 minutes?
options: About 0.43 s, so the timestamps option (PAWS) is needed
About 3.4 s, so an old duplicate segment could still be in the network after the numbers wrap, and the timestamps option (PAWS) is needed
About 34 s, so wrap-around is not a concern
About 3.4 s, but wrap-around is harmless because every segment has a checksum
questions.explanation: 2^32 bytes × 8 = 3.44 × 10^10 bits, and 3.44 × 10^10 / 10^10 bit/s ≈ 3.4 s, far less than the 120 s MSL, so a delayed old segment could carry a sequence number that is valid again. PAWS (RFC 7323) uses TCP timestamps to reject such segments; 0.43 s forgets that sequence numbers count bytes, not bits.

questions.questionText: An Ethernet link has an MTU of 1,500 bytes. With 20-byte IPv4 and 20-byte TCP headers (no options), what MSS should a host announce?
questions.explanation: The MSS counts only TCP data: MSS = MTU − IP header − TCP header = 1,500 − 20 − 20 = 1,460 bytes. 1,480 subtracts only the IP header, and 1,472 is the largest UDP payload (1,500 − 20 − 8).

questions.questionText: Which statement about the TCP maximum segment size (MSS) option is correct?
options: It is sent only in SYN segments and announces the largest amount of data, excluding the TCP and IP headers, that its sender is willing to receive in one segment
It is sent in every segment and gives the current receive window
It limits the total number of segments in the connection
It includes the IP and TCP headers, so it always equals the link MTU
questions.explanation: Each side may state its MSS once, in its SYN, and the other side must not send segments with more data than that; if no MSS option arrives, an IPv4 host assumes 536 bytes. The receive window is a separate header field that changes throughout the connection.

questions.questionText: During the handshake a host announced a window scale shift count of 7, and both sides used the option. A later segment from that host has 65,535 in its 16-bit window field. What receive window does it advertise?
questions.explanation: The true window is the field value shifted left by S bits: 65,535 × 2^7 = 65,535 × 128 = 8,388,480 bytes (about 8 MB). 458,745 multiplies by 7 instead of 2^7, and 16,776,960 uses 2^8.

questions.questionText: A path has a bandwidth of 1 Gbps (10^9 bit/s) and an RTT of 100 ms. The 16-bit window field holds at most 65,535. What is the smallest window scale shift count S the receiver must announce so that its advertised window can cover the bandwidth-delay product and keep the pipe full?
questions.explanation: BDP = 10^9 bit/s × 0.1 s = 10^8 bits = 12,500,000 bytes, and 12,500,000 / 65,535 ≈ 190.7, so 2^S must be at least 190.7, giving S = 8 (2^7 = 128 is too small). S = 11 comes from forgetting to convert bits to bytes, and 14 is only the largest shift allowed.

questions.questionText: Which SCTP feature avoids TCP's head-of-line blocking, in which one lost segment delays the delivery of all later data?
options: The four-way handshake with a state cookie
questions.explanation: SCTP can carry several independent streams in one association, each with its own ordering, so a loss on one stream does not hold back messages on the others. Multi-homing gives failover between IP addresses, and the cookie handshake protects against SYN-flood style attacks.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing TCP and UDP is NOT correct?
options: UDP can be used for broadcast and multicast, while TCP cannot
The minimum TCP header is 20 bytes, while the UDP header is always 8 bytes
TCP provides congestion control, while UDP leaves it to the application
UDP provides flow control through a window field in its header
questions.explanation: The UDP header has only ports, length and checksum, with no window field, so UDP has no flow control. The other three statements are true: TCP is point-to-point only, its header is 20 to 60 bytes, and it runs congestion control.

questions.questionText: On-demand video services such as Netflix commonly stream over HTTP on TCP, whereas video calls use RTP over UDP. Why is TCP acceptable for on-demand streaming?
options: A UDP datagram cannot carry more than 512 bytes, which is too small for video
TCP never needs to retransmit video data
The player buffers several seconds of video ahead, so occasional retransmission delays are hidden, and HTTP over TCP passes easily through firewalls, NAT and web caches
TCP always has lower delay than UDP
questions.explanation: Because playback runs seconds behind the download, a retransmitted segment still arrives before it is needed, so reliability costs nothing visible, and ordinary HTTP delivery works well with CDNs and middleboxes. A live call has no such buffer, which is why it uses UDP.

questions.questionText: A TCP receiver finds that an arriving segment fails its checksum. What happens?
options: The receiver discards the segment; because it is not acknowledged, the sender retransmits it after a timeout or duplicate ACKs
The receiver corrects the damaged bits using the checksum
The receiver passes the data to the application with an error flag
The receiver immediately resets the connection with RST
questions.explanation: The Internet checksum can only detect errors, so the damaged segment is silently dropped. The missing acknowledgement makes the sender resend the data, which is how TCP recovers from errors: by retransmission.

questions.questionText: An application writes 4,000 bytes to a TCP connection whose next data byte is numbered 10,001. The MSS is 1,460 bytes and the sender uses full-sized segments. What are the sequence numbers of the segments, and which ACK number acknowledges all of the data?
questions.explanation: The segments carry 1,460, 1,460 and 1,080 bytes (bytes 10,001 to 11,460, 11,461 to 12,920 and 12,921 to 14,000), so they start at 10,001, 11,461 and 12,921, and the final ACK is the next byte expected, 14,001. Numbering the segments 10,001, 10,002 and 10,003 is the classic mistake: TCP numbers bytes.

subtopics.title: Ports, Sockets, Multiplexing & Demultiplexing
subtopics.subtitle: Port ranges, well-known ports, sockets, the 4-tuple, mux/demux and NAT port translation

concepts.text: Port Numbers

A port number is a 16-bit identifier that the transport layer uses to name a process (or service) on a host. Because it is 16 bits, there are 2^16 = 65,536 ports, numbered 0 to 65535, and TCP and UDP each have their own independent set. IANA divides the range into three parts. Servers normally listen on fixed, well-known ports, while clients use temporary ports chosen by the operating system.

rows: Assigned by IANA to standard services; binding usually needs admin/root rights
Registered with IANA for specific applications (e.g. 3306 MySQL, 3389 RDP, 8080 HTTP alternate)
Not assigned; picked temporarily by client operating systems

concepts.text: More well-known ports worth memorising:
items: 69 TFTP (UDP), 110 POP3 (TCP), 143 IMAP (TCP), 123 NTP (UDP).
161 SNMP agent and 162 SNMP trap (UDP), 179 BGP (TCP), 520 RIP (UDP).
993 IMAPS and 995 POP3S (TCP, mail over TLS), 587 SMTP submission.

concepts.text: Sockets and the Connection 4-Tuple

A socket address is the combination of an IP address and a port number, for example 192.168.1.10:51234; it uniquely identifies one endpoint of communication. In programming, a socket is also the operating-system object (created by socket()) through which an application sends and receives data. A TCP connection is identified by a pair of sockets, that is, the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port); together with the protocol number this is often called the 5-tuple.

concepts.plainText: Connection = (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol)

concepts.text: Multiplexing and Demultiplexing

Multiplexing happens at the sender: the transport layer gathers data from many application processes (through their sockets), adds a header with source and destination port numbers to each chunk, and passes the segments to the single IP layer. Demultiplexing happens at the receiver: the transport layer examines the header fields of each arriving segment and delivers the data to the correct socket. This many-to-one then one-to-many arrangement lets a browser, an e-mail client and a video call share one IP address at the same time.

rows: 4-tuple: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port
Segments from different clients to same port
Go to different sockets (one per connection)
Listening socket plus a new socket per accepted connection

concepts.text: Example: a web server at 203.0.113.5 listens on TCP port 80. Client A (10.0.0.2) opens two browser tabs using ephemeral ports 50001 and 50002, and client B (10.0.0.3) also happens to use port 50001. The three connections are (10.0.0.2, 50001, 203.0.113.5, 80), (10.0.0.2, 50002, 203.0.113.5, 80) and (10.0.0.3, 50001, 203.0.113.5, 80). All share destination port 80, but each 4-tuple is different, so the server demultiplexes them to three separate connection sockets.
Ephemeral ports and port translation:
items: An ephemeral port is a short-lived client port assigned automatically by the OS when a client connects; IANA suggests 49152 to 65535, although Linux uses 32768 to 60999 by default.
NAT (Network Address Translation) rewrites private source IP addresses to a public address at the router.

PAT / NAPT (port address translation, NAT overload) also rewrites the source port, so thousands of private hosts share one public IP; the router keeps a table mapping (private IP, private port) to (public IP, public port).
Port forwarding is the reverse: a fixed public port on the router is mapped to an internal server's IP and port.

concepts.text:
$ netstat -an
Proto Local Address        Foreign Address      State
TCP   0.0.0.0:80           0.0.0.0:0            LISTENING
TCP   192.168.1.10:51234   142.250.1.100:443    ESTABLISHED
UDP   0.0.0.0:53           *:*

The netstat (or ss on Linux) command lists each socket with its local address:port, foreign address:port and TCP state, which is a direct view of the 4-tuples the transport layer uses for demultiplexing.
Going Deeper: Ports, Sockets and Demultiplexing

If an IP address is the street address of an apartment building, a port number is the flat number inside it: the network layer brings the packet to the right building (host), and the transport layer hands it to the right flat (process). The transport layer also works like a mail sorting office: outgoing letters from many residents are collected, labelled and sent out together (multiplexing), and incoming letters are sorted and delivered to the right door (demultiplexing). A socket address such as 192.168.1.5:80 names both at once: the computer at 192.168.1.5 and the web-server process on port 80 there.
Notes on the common port list:
items: DNS uses port 53 over both UDP and TCP: UDP for ordinary queries, TCP for zone transfers and for answers too large for one UDP message. DNS over TLS uses TCP port 853.
FTP uses two connections: port 21 for control and, in active mode, port 20 for data; in passive mode the server picks a high data port.
SMTP on port 25 relays mail between servers, while mail clients submit new mail on port 587 (with STARTTLS) or 465 (implicit TLS); POP3 (110) and IMAP (143) are for reading mail.

Services with implicit TLS have their own ports: HTTPS 443, IMAPS 993, POP3S 995 and LDAPS 636. Telnet (23) normally sends everything, passwords included, in clear text, which is why SSH (22) has replaced it.
A port is a number in software that names an application endpoint; it has nothing to do with the physical sockets (jacks) on a computer or switch.

HTTP alternate, proxies and test servers

concepts.text:
import socket
# Server program: socket -> bind -> listen -> accept -> recv/send -> close
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))        # claim local port 8080 on every address
srv.listen(5)                      # passive socket, backlog of 5
conn, addr = srv.accept()          # blocks; returns a new socket per client
conn.sendall(conn.recv(1024))      # echo one message back
conn.close()
# Client program (run separately): socket -> connect -> send/recv -> close
cli = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
cli.connect(("192.0.2.10", 8080))  # OS picks an ephemeral port, sends SYN
cli.sendall(b"hello")
print(cli.recv(1024))
cli.close()

bind() attaches a socket to a local IP address and port; a server must call it to claim its well-known port, while a client normally skips it and lets connect() pick an ephemeral port. listen() turns the socket into a passive listening socket with a queue (backlog) of connections whose handshake has completed, and accept() takes the next one from that queue and returns a brand-new socket for it. The new socket has the same local port as the listening socket but its own remote IP address and port, so every client has its own 4-tuple. A UDP server needs only socket() and bind(), and then uses recvfrom() and sendto() on that single socket for every client.

UDP 10.0.0.8:61000 -> 10.0.0.1:53         S1 (same socket, whatever the source)
TCP 10.0.0.7:40000 -> 10.0.0.1:80, data   S3 (the full 4-tuple matches)
TCP 10.0.0.8:40000 -> 10.0.0.1:80, SYN    S2 (no connection matches; accept() makes S4)

concepts.text: Special cases and common mistakes:
items: Binding to 0.0.0.0 (INADDR_ANY) means 'every local address'; binding to 127.0.0.1 accepts only connections made from the same machine.

Normally only one socket at a time may bind a given IP address, port and protocol; a second bind() fails with 'Address already in use' (EADDRINUSE) unless options such as SO_REUSEADDR or SO_REUSEPORT change the rules.
Binding to port 0 asks the OS for any free port, and getsockname() reveals which one was chosen.
On Linux, by default only root or a process with the CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability may bind a port below 1024.

Ephemeral ranges differ: IANA and Windows use 49152 to 65535 (16,384 ports), while Linux defaults to 32768 to 60999 (28,232 ports). An actively closed connection keeps its port in TIME_WAIT for a while, so a client that opens connections very quickly to one server socket can run out of ports.
The listening socket and all of its accepted sockets share one local port; they differ only in the remote IP address and port.

concepts.text: In a demultiplexing question, check the protocol first, because TCP and UDP ports are separate. For UDP match only the destination IP address and port; for TCP match the full 4-tuple first, and only a SYN that matches no existing connection goes to the listening socket.

Dynamic/ephemeral range 49152 to 65535 contains 16384 ports
Socket address = IP address : port number

notes.text: UDP demultiplexes on destination IP and port only; TCP uses the full 4-tuple. That is why one TCP server port (80) can carry thousands of simultaneous connections.
TCP port 53 and UDP port 53 are different ports: the protocol number is part of the identity, so a host can run separate TCP and UDP services on the same number.
Do not mix up the ranges: registered ports end at 49151 and dynamic ports start at 49152. Port 1023 is the last well-known port.

flashcards.front: What is demultiplexing at the transport layer?
flashcards.back: At the receiver, the transport layer reads the port numbers (and for TCP the full 4-tuple) in each segment and delivers the data to the correct application socket.

flashcards.front: What is the registered port range?
flashcards.back: 1024 to 49151; these ports are registered with IANA for specific applications such as 3306 (MySQL) and 3389 (RDP).
A temporary client-side port chosen automatically by the operating system for the duration of a connection, typically from 49152 to 65535.

flashcards.front: How does PAT let many hosts share one public IP address?
flashcards.back: The router rewrites each outgoing packet's source IP and source port to its public IP and a unique port, and keeps a translation table to map replies back.

questions.questionText: A web server on TCP port 80 has many clients connected at the same time. Which fields does TCP use to deliver each incoming segment to the correct connection socket?
options: Destination IP address and destination port only
Source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port
questions.explanation: A TCP connection socket is identified by the 4-tuple, so segments from different clients to the same port 80 go to different sockets. UDP uses only the destination IP and port.

questions.questionText: How many port numbers are in the IANA dynamic/private (ephemeral) range?
questions.explanation: The dynamic range is 49152 to 65535, which is 65535 - 49152 + 1 = 16384 ports.

questions.questionText: Which port does FTP use for its control connection?
questions.explanation: FTP keeps its control connection, which carries commands and replies, on TCP port 21, and moves files over a separate data connection (port 20 in active mode, a server-chosen high port in passive mode). Port 22 is SSH and 23 is Telnet.

questions.questionText: In the socket address 192.168.1.5:80, what do the two parts identify?
options: The network address and the subnet mask of the host
The MAC address and the IP address of the host
The host's IP address, and the port of the process on that host (here a web server)
The IP address of the default router and the number of hops to the host
questions.explanation: A socket address is an IP address plus a port number: 192.168.1.5 selects the computer, and port 80 selects the application on it, normally a web server (HTTP). MAC addresses and subnet masks are not part of a socket address.

questions.questionText: What is the function of multiplexing at the transport layer?
options: To combine several subnets into one LAN
To send the same data to every host on the network
To encrypt the data of several applications with one key
To let many application processes on a host send data through the one network layer at the same time, with each chunk labelled by port numbers
questions.explanation: At the sender, the transport layer collects data from many sockets, adds a header with source and destination ports to each chunk and passes all the segments to IP. The port numbers are what later let the receiver separate the streams again (demultiplexing).

questions.questionText: Which of these well-known ports belongs to a service that is encrypted with TLS from the very first byte (implicit TLS), as HTTPS on port 443 is?
questions.explanation: 993 is IMAPS, that is IMAP over TLS, just as 443 is HTTP over TLS. IMAP on 143 and POP3 on 110 start in clear text (they can upgrade with STARTTLS), and Telnet on 23 normally sends everything, passwords included, in clear text.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between multiplexing and demultiplexing at the transport layer?
options: Multiplexing, at the sender, gathers data from many sockets into segments for the network layer; demultiplexing, at the receiver, uses the header fields to deliver each segment to the correct socket
Multiplexing encrypts data, while demultiplexing decrypts it
Multiplexing is done only by TCP, while demultiplexing is done only by UDP
Multiplexing works only with IPv6, while demultiplexing works only with IPv4
questions.explanation: Both happen in TCP and in UDP, over IPv4 or IPv6: the sender merges many application streams into one flow of segments (many to one), and the receiver splits them again by port numbers (one to many). It is like a mail sorting office that collects outgoing letters and distributes incoming ones.

questions.questionText: Port numbers are carried in 16-bit fields of the TCP and UDP headers. How many different values can such a field hold, and what is the highest port number?
questions.explanation: A 16-bit field holds 2^16 = 65,536 values, numbered 0 to 65,535 (port 0 itself is reserved). 1,024 is only the size of the well-known range, 0 to 1,023.

questions.questionText: MySQL listens on TCP port 3306 and Remote Desktop (RDP) on TCP port 3389. In which IANA port range do these ports lie?
questions.explanation: 3306 and 3389 lie between 1024 and 49151, the registered range, in which IANA records ports for specific applications. The well-known range ends at 1023 and the dynamic range starts at 49152.

questions.questionText: In the study analogy in which an IP address is like the street address of an apartment building, what does the port number correspond to?
options: The city in which the building stands
The postman who carries the letter
The flat (apartment) number of the resident inside the building
questions.explanation: The IP address gets the data to the right building (host), and the port number picks the right flat inside it, that is, the right application process on the host.

questions.questionText: At the transport layer, what is a port number?
options: A physical connector (jack) on the network interface card
The hardware address burned into the network card
A 16-bit logical number that identifies an application endpoint, such as a process or service, on a host
The number of the router interface that a packet leaves from
questions.explanation: A transport-layer port is a logical number in software (0 to 65,535) that tells TCP or UDP which process should receive the data; it has nothing to do with the physical sockets on a card or switch. The hardware address is the MAC address, used at the data link layer.

questions.questionText: A browser using source port 51500 sends a request to an HTTPS server. Which source and destination ports does the server's reply segment carry?
questions.explanation: The reply swaps the two ports: it comes from the server's port 443 and goes to the client's ephemeral port 51500, which the client's transport layer uses to find the browser's socket.

questions.questionText: Which socket call makes a TCP client send the SYN segment that starts the three-way handshake?
questions.explanation: connect() performs the active open: the client's TCP sends a SYN, and the call returns once the handshake completes or fails. bind() only assigns a local address, listen() makes a server socket passive, and send() needs an existing connection.

questions.questionText: An e-mail client submits outgoing mail to its provider's server and protects the session with STARTTLS. Which TCP port does this mail submission normally use?
questions.explanation: Port 587 is the mail submission port (RFC 6409), used by clients with STARTTLS; port 465 is the implicit-TLS alternative. Port 25 is for relaying between servers, 110 is POP3 and 993 is IMAPS, both for reading mail.

questions.questionText: Which list gives the well-known ports of SMTP, DNS, SNMP (agent queries) and NTP, in that order?
questions.explanation: SMTP uses TCP 25, DNS uses 53, SNMP agents receive queries on UDP 161 and NTP uses UDP 123. 162 is the SNMP trap port, 119 is NNTP, 110 is POP3 and 69 is TFTP.

questions.questionText: DNS normally answers queries over UDP port 53. When does DNS use TCP port 53 instead?
options: Only when the client is behind a NAT router
For zone transfers between servers and for responses too large for a single UDP message
For every query sent to a root server
Never; DNS is defined only over UDP
questions.explanation: Zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR) and truncated answers (TC bit set) are carried over TCP 53, and RFC 7766 requires DNS software to support TCP. Short queries stay on UDP because a single request and reply need no connection setup.

questions.questionText: A client program calls connect() on a TCP socket without calling bind() first. Which statement about its source port is correct?
options: The operating system automatically assigns an unused ephemeral port
The source port is set equal to the destination port
The source port stays 0 for the whole connection
connect() fails, because bind() is mandatory for clients
questions.explanation: If the socket is unbound, connect() makes the OS bind it implicitly to a free ephemeral port (for example from 49152 to 65535, or 32768 to 60999 on Linux). Clients rarely call bind() because they do not need a fixed port.

questions.questionText: A UDP server has one unconnected socket bound to port 5000. Clients at 10.0.0.2:40000 and 10.0.0.3:40000 each send it a datagram. How does UDP demultiplex them?
options: Each datagram goes to a new socket created for its sender, as with TCP's accept()
The second datagram is dropped because both clients use source port 40000
The two datagrams are merged into a single message before delivery
Both go to the same socket, because UDP matches only the destination IP address and port; the application learns each sender from recvfrom()
questions.explanation: A UDP socket is identified by its destination IP address and port only, so every datagram for port 5000 reaches the same socket, whatever its source. recvfrom() returns each sender's address so that the server can reply with sendto().

questions.questionText: Host 10.0.0.1 has three sockets: S1 is a UDP socket bound to port 53, S2 is a TCP socket listening on port 80, and S3 is a TCP connection between 10.0.0.1:80 and 10.0.0.5:45000. Three packets arrive: (i) a TCP data segment from 10.0.0.5:45000 to port 80, (ii) a TCP SYN from 10.0.0.6:45000 to port 80, and (iii) a UDP datagram from 10.0.0.5:45000 to port 53. Which sockets receive (i), (ii) and (iii)?
questions.explanation: Segment (i) matches S3's full 4-tuple; the SYN in (ii) matches no connection because its source IP differs, so it goes to the listening socket S2, which will create a new connection socket; and (iii) is UDP, so only the destination port 53 matters and it goes to S1. Matching on the source port alone, or ignoring the protocol, gives the wrong answers.

questions.questionText: In what order does a typical TCP server call the socket API functions before it can exchange data with a client?
questions.explanation: The server creates the socket, binds it to its well-known address and port, marks it passive with listen() and then calls accept(), which waits for a client and returns a new connected socket. connect() is the client's call.

questions.questionText: On a Linux server with default settings, a program running as an ordinary (non-root) user calls bind() on TCP port 80. What happens?
options: bind() succeeds, because any user may use any port
bind() succeeds, but the port is silently changed to 8080
bind() fails, because port 80 is reserved for UDP
bind() fails with a permission error, because ports below 1024 need root or the CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability
questions.explanation: By default Linux treats the well-known ports 0 to 1023 as privileged, so only root or a process with CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE may bind them, and bind() returns EACCES otherwise. This is why development servers often use a registered port such as 8080 instead.

questions.questionText: Can a host run a TCP service and a separate UDP service on port 5000 at the same time?
options: Yes; TCP and UDP have independent port spaces, and the IP protocol field tells the host which one a packet is for
No; a port number can be bound only once per host, whatever the protocol
Only if both services run in the same process
Only if the port number is above 49151
questions.explanation: A port is always a TCP port or a UDP port: the host first looks at the IP Protocol field (6 or 17) and only then at the port number. DNS relies on exactly this, serving UDP 53 and TCP 53 side by side.

questions.questionText: Server 10.0.0.1 runs a TCP web server on port 80 and a DNS server that uses one unconnected UDP socket on port 53. Client A (10.0.0.2) has two browser connections open to port 80 and sends DNS queries from UDP port 51000; client B (10.0.0.3) has one browser connection open and also sends DNS queries from UDP port 51000. How many sockets are in use on the server?
questions.explanation: TCP needs the listening socket plus one connected socket per connection, 1 + 3 = 4, while UDP needs only the one socket on port 53 for all clients, so the total is 4 + 1 = 5. 3 counts only the connections, and 6 wrongly gives each UDP client its own socket.

questions.questionText:
netstat on a PC shows these two lines:

TCP  0.0.0.0:3389      0.0.0.0:0           LISTENING
TCP  10.1.1.25:59876   93.184.216.34:443   ESTABLISHED

Which statement is correct?
options: The PC is running an HTTPS server on port 59876
Port 3389 is the ephemeral port chosen for the HTTPS connection
The PC accepts Remote Desktop connections on all of its addresses, and it is also a client of an HTTPS server, using ephemeral port 59876
The PC accepts Remote Desktop connections only from the host 0.0.0.0
questions.explanation: 0.0.0.0:3389 LISTENING is an RDP server socket bound to every local address; the ESTABLISHED line pairs the local ephemeral port 59876 with the remote port 443, so the PC is the HTTPS client. 0.0.0.0 in the local address column means 'any local address', not a remote host.

questions.questionText: A developer's test server binds its TCP socket to 127.0.0.1:8000. A colleague's computer on the LAN then tries to connect to the server machine's LAN address on port 8000 (no firewall is involved). What happens?
options: The connection succeeds, because the port number matches
The connection is refused (the host answers with RST), because the socket accepts only connections addressed to the loopback address
The router automatically forwards the connection to 127.0.0.1
The connection succeeds, but only for UDP traffic
questions.explanation: Binding to 127.0.0.1 limits the socket to packets addressed to the loopback interface, so a SYN addressed to the LAN IP finds no matching socket and TCP replies with RST ('connection refused'). Binding to 0.0.0.0 or to the LAN address would accept it.

questions.questionText:
What does this Python program print?

import socket
a = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
a.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
port = a.getsockname()[1]
a.listen()
b = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
try:
    b.bind(("127.0.0.1", port))
    print("bound")
except OSError:
    print("in use")
options: Nothing: the program blocks at listen()
questions.explanation: Binding to port 0 lets the OS choose a free port, which getsockname() reveals; a second socket cannot bind the same address and port while the first holds it, so bind() raises OSError (EADDRINUSE, 'Address already in use'). listen() does not block; only accept() waits.

questions.questionText:
What does this Python program print?

import socket
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
srv.listen()
port = srv.getsockname()[1]
c1 = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port))
c2 = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port))
s1, _ = srv.accept()
s2, _ = srv.accept()
print(s1.getsockname()[1] == port,
      s2.getsockname()[1] == port,
      s1.getpeername()[1] == s2.getpeername()[1])
questions.explanation: Sockets returned by accept() keep the server's local port, so the first two tests are True, but the two clients were given different ephemeral source ports, so the last test is False. The two 4-tuples therefore differ, which is how TCP demultiplexes both connections on one server port.

questions.questionText: A home router with public address 198.51.100.9 has a port-forwarding rule: TCP 8443 to 192.168.1.20:443. An outside client at 203.0.113.50:52000 connects to 198.51.100.9:8443. When the router passes the SYN onto the LAN, what are its destination and source socket addresses? (The router translates only the destination.)
questions.explanation: Port forwarding (destination NAT) rewrites the destination socket from 198.51.100.9:8443 to 192.168.1.20:443 and leaves the client's source socket unchanged, so the server sees the real client address. The router records the mapping and reverses it on the server's replies.

questions.questionText: Inside hosts 192.168.1.10 and 192.168.1.11 both open TCP connections from source port 50000 to 93.184.216.34:443 through a PAT router whose public address is 203.0.113.5. The router maps the first connection to public port 62000 and the second to 62001. A reply arrives from 93.184.216.34:443 addressed to 203.0.113.5:62001. After translation, what are the reply's source and destination socket addresses?
questions.explanation: Public port 62001 belongs to the second mapping, so the router rewrites the destination back to 192.168.1.11:50000 and leaves the server's source socket untouched. The different public ports are what let PAT tell apart two inside hosts that happened to pick the same private port.

questions.questionText: Which statement about sockets and TCP connections is NOT correct?
options: A TCP connection is identified by the pair of socket addresses at its two ends
A server's listening socket and the sockets returned by accept() all use the same local port
A client may hold several connections to the same server port at once, each from a different source port
Two simultaneous TCP connections on one host may have the same 4-tuple if they belong to different processes
questions.explanation: The 4-tuple is what identifies a connection, so two live connections can never share one, whichever processes own them. The other statements are true: accepted sockets share the server port, and a browser can open many connections to port 443 from different ephemeral ports.

questions.questionText: A load-testing client has 2 IP addresses and uses the ephemeral port range 32768 to 60999. It opens TCP connections to one server IP address on ports 80 and 443. If the only limit is that every connection's 4-tuple must be unique, what is the maximum number of simultaneous connections?
questions.explanation: The range holds 60,999 − 32,768 + 1 = 28,232 ports, and every (client IP, server port) pair can use all of them: 28,232 × 2 × 2 = 112,928 connections. 56,464 applies only one of the two factors of 2, and 262,144 wrongly uses all 65,536 ports.

questions.questionText: A client with one IP address uses the ephemeral range 32768 to 60999 and keeps opening short TCP connections to the same server socket, closing each one itself (active close). Each closed connection keeps its port in TIME_WAIT for 60 s, and a port is not reused until TIME_WAIT ends. What is the highest connection rate the client can sustain?
questions.explanation: Each connection ties up one of the 60,999 − 32,768 + 1 = 28,232 ports for about 60 s, so at most 28,232 / 60 ≈ 470.5, about 470 new connections per second, can be sustained. 1,092 uses all 65,536 ports, 273 uses the 16,384-port IANA range, and 235 assumes that TIME_WAIT lasts 120 s.

subtopics.subtitle: Three-way handshake, ISN, SYN flood, FIN release, TIME_WAIT and the TCP state machine

concepts.text: Three-Way Handshake

TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake so that both sides agree to communicate and learn each other's initial sequence number (ISN). The server first does a passive open (it listens on a port); the client performs an active open by sending a SYN. The SYN and SYN-ACK segments carry no data, but each consumes one sequence number. Options such as maximum segment size (MSS), window scale and SACK permission are negotiated in these segments.
Handshake steps (client ISN = x, server ISN = y):
items: Step 1, client to server: SYN = 1, seq = x. Client moves to SYN_SENT.
Step 2, server to client: SYN = 1, ACK = 1, seq = y, ack = x + 1. Server moves to SYN_RCVD.
Step 3, client to server: ACK = 1, seq = x + 1, ack = y + 1. Both sides are now ESTABLISHED and data may flow (this ACK may already carry data).

concepts.plainText: SYN seq = x; SYN-ACK seq = y, ack = x + 1; ACK ack = y + 1

concepts.text: The ISN is not zero; it is chosen pseudo-randomly (historically from a clock ticking every 4 microseconds, now combined with a hash of the 4-tuple and a secret, RFC 6528). Random ISNs prevent delayed segments from an old connection with the same 4-tuple being accepted as new data, and make it hard for an attacker to guess sequence numbers and hijack or spoof a connection.
SYN flood attack and SYN cookies:
items: In a SYN flood (a denial-of-service attack) the attacker sends many SYNs, often with spoofed source addresses, and never sends the final ACK.
Each half-open connection occupies an entry in the server's backlog (SYN_RCVD queue) until it times out, so legitimate clients are refused.
SYN cookies defend by storing no state: the server encodes the connection details (a hash of the 4-tuple, a timestamp and the MSS) into its ISN y.
Only when a valid ACK arrives with ack = y + 1 does the server rebuild the state from the cookie and create the connection.

concepts.text: Connection Release

A TCP connection is full duplex, so each direction is closed separately, usually in four segments. The side that closes first (active close) sends FIN; the other side ACKs it and enters CLOSE_WAIT, where it may still send data. When that application also closes, it sends its own FIN, and the active closer ACKs it. The second and third segments can be combined into one FIN+ACK, giving a three-segment release. Like SYN, each FIN consumes one sequence number.
Special closing cases:
items: Half-close: one side stops sending (sends FIN) but continues to receive, for example a client that has sent all its input and waits for the result (shutdown() in sockets).
Simultaneous close: both sides send FIN at the same time; each goes FIN_WAIT_1 to CLOSING to TIME_WAIT.
Abort with RST: a segment with RST = 1 ends the connection at once, discarding buffered data; it is also sent in reply to a SYN for a port where nothing is listening.

concepts.text: After sending the final ACK, the active closer stays in TIME_WAIT for 2 MSL (twice the maximum segment lifetime, commonly 2 x 30 s to 2 x 2 min). This serves two purposes: if the last ACK is lost, the peer retransmits its FIN and the endpoint is still there to re-send the ACK; and it lets any delayed duplicate segments of this connection die out before the same 4-tuple can be reused by a new connection.
